\chapter{Clients, Documents and Data}
\label{ch:cliente-documento-dato-impreso-rellenar}
\hlchaptermodality{406}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can understand a basic form and say that a client fills in a document with data.}

Retrieve the five form-and-document words in one practical instruction.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el cliente, la cliente]{el cliente, la cliente — the person on the other side of the counter}

\label{lesson:ES-C406-cliente}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the shop}. (\emph{La tienda}.) Now name the person who buys there: \textbf{el cliente} or \textbf{la cliente}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Cliente} comes from Latin \textbf{cliens}, a person connected to and protected by a patron. The relationship changed over time. In modern Spanish, a \textbf{cliente} is a customer of a shop or a client who uses a professional service.

The word itself can stay the same for a man or a woman; the article does the work: \textbf{el cliente}, \textbf{la cliente}. You may also meet \textbf{clienta} for a woman.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: meaning in a scene}]
Picture a counter. One person works for the shop; the other asks for a product or service. That second person is \textbf{el cliente} or \textbf{la cliente}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{el cliente de la tienda} — the shop's customer
  \item \textbf{la cliente necesita ayuda} — the customer needs help
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el cliente}
  \item \emph{la cliente}
  \item \emph{el cliente de la tienda}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the customer or client? (\emph{El cliente; la cliente}.)

Source: \href{https://dle.rae.es/cliente}{DLE: cliente}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el documento]{el documento — a paper that shows or proves}

\label{lesson:ES-C406-documento}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the passport} and \emph{the paper}. (\emph{El pasaporte, el papel}.) A passport is one kind of \textbf{documento}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{El documento} comes from Latin \textbf{documentum}, something that gives evidence or instruction. Its deeper verb is \textbf{docēre}, “to teach.” English \textbf{document}, \textbf{doctor}, \textbf{doctrine} and \textbf{docent} belong to the same family: each points to showing, teaching or establishing something.

A \textbf{papel} is the material. A \textbf{documento} is the meaningful record on it — or the digital equivalent. A passport is both a small book and an official \textbf{documento}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: useful combinations}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{el documento de identidad} — the identity document
  \item \textbf{el pasaporte es un documento} — the passport is a document
  \item \textbf{necesito el documento} — I need the document
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el documento}
  \item \emph{el documento de identidad}
  \item \emph{el pasaporte es un documento}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What written record can serve as proof? (\emph{El documento}.)

Source: \href{https://dle.rae.es/documento}{DLE: documento}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el dato]{el dato — one thing given as information}

\label{lesson:ES-C406-dato}



\begin{quote}
A form may ask for your name and address: \emph{el nombre, la dirección}. Each answer is \textbf{un dato}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Dato} comes straight from Latin \textbf{datum}, “something given.” English kept \textbf{datum} for one item and \textbf{data} for several; Spanish made the everyday noun \textbf{el dato}, plural \textbf{los datos}.

A name, address or telephone number can each be \textbf{un dato}. Together they are \textbf{los datos personales}, personal details.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one or several}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{un dato} — one piece of information
  \item \textbf{los datos} — the information / details
  \item \textbf{nombre y dirección: dos datos} — name and address: two details
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{un dato}
  \item \emph{los datos}
  \item \emph{los datos personales}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
One piece of information? (\emph{Un dato}.) Several details? (\emph{Los datos}.)

Source: \href{https://dle.rae.es/dato}{DLE: dato}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el impreso]{el impreso — a form waiting for your data}

\label{lesson:ES-C406-impreso}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the document}, \emph{the data} and \emph{the paper}. (\emph{El documento, los datos, el papel}.) Put blank spaces on that paper and you have \textbf{el impreso}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Impreso} is the irregular past participle of \textbf{imprimir}, “to print,” from Latin \textbf{impressus}, “pressed into.” Printing once meant pressing inked type onto paper. English \textbf{impress} preserves the same image.

As a noun, \textbf{el impreso} can mean a printed sheet, especially a form with blank spaces for a procedure. In much of the Spanish-speaking world you will also hear \textbf{el formulario}. Here the exam-derived word is \textbf{impreso}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a form has two sides}]
The \textbf{impreso} supplies the labels; you supply \textbf{los datos}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Nombre:} Ana
  \item \textbf{Dirección:} Calle Sol, 4
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el impreso}
  \item \emph{los datos del impreso}
  \item \emph{el documento y el impreso}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What printed sheet waits for your details? (\emph{El impreso}.) What do you put in it? (\emph{Los datos}.)

Source: \href{https://dle.rae.es/impreso}{DLE: impreso}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rellenar]{rellenar — fill the blanks with what they need}

\label{lesson:ES-C406-rellenar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the form}, \emph{the data} and \emph{full}. (\emph{El impreso, los datos, lleno}.) The action that connects them is \textbf{rellenar}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Rellenar} shows its construction on the surface: \textbf{re-} + \textbf{llenar}, “to fill.” Its broad sense is to fill something again or completely. In an office, it has the practical meaning “to fill in” or “to fill out.”

The DLE gives the form sense precisely: putting the necessary data into blank spaces in forms or documents. That is why the noun chain from this chapter ends in an action:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{rellenar el impreso con los datos}
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a regular -ar action}]
You already know the regular \textbf{-ar} machine:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{relleno el impreso} — I fill in the form
  \item \textbf{rellena el impreso} — he/she fills in the form; fill in the form
\end{itemize}

The noun \textbf{relleno} can also mean a filling, but the sentence and article tell you what job the form is doing.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{rellenar}
  \item \emph{rellenar el impreso}
  \item \emph{rellenar el impreso con los datos}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \emph{to fill in the form with the data}. (\emph{Rellenar el impreso con los datos}.)

Source: \href{https://dle.rae.es/rellenar}{DLE: rellenar}.
\end{tcolorbox}
